article.articleHeadline: Ebola continues to ravage the DRC - 828 people have died.
article.articleSummary:
- As of the latest tally, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is 2,124 laboratory-confirmed cases with 828 deaths. Officially announced on May 15, the outbreak is spreading faster than previous ones, with confirmed cases exceeding 2,000 within two months, versus over ten months in 2018. The 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no vaccine or treatment. Ebola causes hemorrhagic fever and has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past five decades. The most deadly DRC outbreak (2018–2020) reported about 2,300 deaths among 3,500 cases.
- Ebola virus disease outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri Province) at Nyankunde Hospital. On 2026-07-17, patients with Ebola fever and healthcare workers fled the facility after a mob attacked the hospital; relatives of a woman who died in childbirth from severe anemia pelted the building, damaged fencing, and prompted abandonment. A hospital biologist noted that blood transfusion is prohibited during Ebola outbreaks, limiting care. Following the attack, staff evacuated; a generator failed, power cut, and several Ebola patients escaped. As of 17 July 2026, Reuters reports 2,073 confirmed Ebola cases in the DRC and 796 deaths. - On July 15, 2026, in Nyankunde, 45 km southwest of Bunia in Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of Congo, security incidents disrupted the Ebola response: militiamen clashed near the Ebola Treatment Center and angry locals pelted its buildings, causing panic. A militiaman leader reportedly died. Four Ebola patients initially fled the center but later returned; one suspected case fled. On July 16, medical response teams from WHO, Africa CDC, and Samaritan’s Purse evacuated Nyankunde for Bunia, reducing on-ground response capacity. The exact circumstances remain unclear. Officials warn that ongoing insecurity prevents health workers from accessing the area, risking delays in outbreak response and potentially impacting control of the Ebola outbreak in the region.
- Two separate violent incidents targeted the Ebola Treatment Center in Nyankunde, Democratic Republic of Congo, exacerbating the Ebola response. Local militiamen fired on the Nyankunde center, with one of their leaders killed. In a separate confrontation, the death of a pregnant woman at the medical center sparked anger and stone-throwing at the facility. Panic led four Ebola patients to flee, though all four later returned; one suspected case fled. On Thursday morning, WHO, Africa CDC, and Samaritan's Purse personnel evacuated Nyankunde for Bunia, leaving about 15 responders. Dr. Yap Boum of Africa CDC warned that unsafe security conditions hinder outbreak response, risking limited access to the health zone and potentially impeding transmission control in areas with significant case loads.
- As of 17 July 2026, the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has 2,073 reported cases and 796 deaths, according to World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. In a briefing at WHO headquarters, he said the current outbreak is the third-largest Ebola outbreak recorded in the DRC and that transmission has accelerated over the past month, faster than during any previous outbreak. The report highlights ongoing transmission and high mortality, though the article does not specify the affected provinces or cities within the DRC, or list common symptoms. The rapid rise underscores a substantial and evolving public health crisis in the region.

The UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expresses serious concern over Israel's decision to grant city status to the West Bank settlement of Givat Ze'ev, noting it does not change the area's legal status and that settlements, including East Jerusalem, violate international law and Security Council resolutions. The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is spreading at unprecedented pace; in the last month there have been 2,073 cases and 796 deaths, with WHO expanding responses and initiating clinical trials of several therapies. Guterres will visit Cyprus July 27–29 to meet Greek- and Turkish-Cypriot leaders, while the Security Council conducts a closed session on Cyprus.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in Haut-Uélé: Protection of the indigenous Pygmy peoples demanded in Isiro - ACP
article.articleSummary: Ebola has been officially declared in Haut-Uélé, in Isiro, Democratic Republic of Congo. Faustin Engwanime Ababu, coordinator of the APCH (Association des Premiers Congolais du Haut-Uélé), appeals for evacuation of protective materials to extend Ebola awareness to indigenous Pygmy camp bases. The association notes Pygmies often rely on traditional remedies and may avoid health facilities, underscoring the need for targeted risk communication and hygiene interventions to halt spread. APCH requests concrete items—buckets, disinfectants, and chlorine—for the Ebola response teams to reach these communities. They plan on-site sensitization drives at pygmy bases but have not yet secured supplies. Ababu also highlights Law No. 22/030 of 15 July 2022, praising its protection of indigenous rights. The appeal emphasizes non-marginalization of pygmies during the outbreak and urges timely support to curb transmission.

article.articleHeadline: Hepatitis-A, typhoid outbreak hits Kaithal village; 47 infected
article.articleSummary: As of 16 July 2026, Sajuma village in Kaithal district has an outbreak of Hepatitis A and typhoid with 47 residents infected this month (35 Hepatitis A, 12 typhoid). Affected individuals were identified after testing 109 residents out of about 1,500 households, with reports corroborating contamination of the drinking water supply. Several patients, including children, were hospitalized last week; a 12-year-old girl died during treatment, with final cause pending confirmation from PGIMER, Chandigarh. Health teams have deployed 24-hour medical teams and ambulances; free consultations, diagnostics and treatments, including liver function tests, Hepatitis A and typhoid checks, are being offered at temporary camps. Officials reviewed the village’s canal-based water project and directed a feasibility study to source drinking water from the Bhakra canal, plus repair/operation of the non-functional RO plant.

article.articleHeadline: Kangra leads Himachal in TB prevention - The Tribune
article.articleSummary: Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh, achieved 91% TB Preventive Treatment (TPT) coverage among eligible household contacts in 2026 under the TB-Mukt Bharat Abhiyan, the highest in the state. Of 1,708 household contacts enrolled, 1,530 were started on TPT, while 34 diagnosed with active tuberculosis were immediately placed on anti-TB therapy. 144 eligible contacts remain to be covered, with plans to reach 95% coverage by enrolling them in the three-month weekly TB Preventive Treatment (3HP) regimen. Kangra’s approach includes systematic household contact investigations, timely chest X-rays and diagnostic evaluations, intensive counseling, real-time monitoring via the Nikshay portal, and close follow-up by frontline health workers. Officials credit coordinated efforts across the TB Centre, medical officers, TB Health Visitors, ASHA workers, pharmacists, and laboratory staff. The achievement reinforces the campaign’s Prevent, Find, Treat and End TB motto and underscores prevention alongside treatment to break transmission in the region.

article.articleHeadline: What are the symptoms of the increasing hand, foot, and mouth disease in children, and what should be done to prevent it?
article.articleSummary: Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease (HFMD), caused by Coxsackie and other enteroviruses, is spreading among children in Karnataka, notably Bengaluru. Transmission occurs via infected saliva, nasal discharge, blister fluid, stool, and contaminated objects—rapid in schools, anganwadis, day-care centers, and playgrounds. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, reduced appetite, malaise, and painful ulcers inside the mouth (tongue, gums, inner cheeks), with red or fluid-filled blisters on hands and feet, sometimes on ankles, knees, or back. Younger children may be irritable and refuse foods or drinks; vomiting can occur. There is no specific antiviral; most recover in 7–10 days with supportive care and doctor-guided fever/pain relief. Prevention emphasizes regular handwashing, cleaning toys and surfaces, isolating the infected child until fully recovered, hygiene before meals and after toileting, and not sharing clothes or towels. Seek urgent care for high fever, excessive drowsiness, severe dehydration, or breathing trouble.

article.articleHeadline: Upper Assam logs 55 JE & 244 AES cases since Jan 1; 11 deaths reported

JE is viral, transmitted by Culex mosquitoes; pigs and wading birds are amplifying hosts; humans are dead-end hosts. Cases rise during monsoon (June–October). Measures include mosquito nets, vaccination drives for children, pig-management, and door-to-door fever surveys, IPC, fogging, and nets distribution.

article.articleHeadline: Why more children are at risk of Hepatitis A despite better hygiene: What parents need to know
article.articleSummary: More than 50% of children aged 1–5 years in India remain vulnerable to Hepatitis A as improved sanitation reduces early exposure, making timely vaccination crucial. Hepatitis A is a viral liver infection spread mainly via contaminated food or water or close contact. Infected children under 6 often have no symptoms; when present, symptoms typically appear 2–6 weeks post-infection and include fever, fatigue, pale stools and dark urine. Most children recover with hydration, nutrition and rest, but relapse can occur for up to 6 months and may require hospitalization in rare cases. The epidemiological shift toward later childhood or adolescence can yield more severe illness, underscoring vaccination as a key prevention strategy. Vaccination is recommended starting at 12 months, with a second dose at 18–19 months to protect before school exposure. Emphasize hand hygiene and vaccination as complementary protections, and advise vigilance for fatigue, loss of appetite, stomach pain or jaundice after local outbreaks in urban and semi-urban India.

District teams collected water and stool samples and sent them to a Cuttack laboratory to identify the causative agent. Health workers are conducting door-to-door surveillance, distributing ORS packets, and advising residents to drink boiled water and maintain hygiene. Officials suspect contaminated drinking water from uncovered wells and storage tanks as the trigger. Adequate medicine stocks exist and preventive measures have been intensified in the affected villages. No lab confirmation yet; the outbreak remains under close surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: ASF outbreak: Kohima bans pig movement
article.articleSummary: African Swine Fever (ASF) has been confirmed in Kohima district, Nagaland, with outbreaks at Peducha Village, Phezoucha L Khel and P Khel of Kohima Village, and the Razha area near Dzü-ü River (NH-29). Deputy Commissioner B Henok Buchem issued containment orders: a 1-km Infected Zone and a 10-km Surveillance Zone. Immediate ban on import, export and movement of live pigs and pork products within, into or out of the zones; all pork markets and butchery shops within zones to close until further notice. Pig farmers must restrict farm visitors, disinfect premises, report unusual pig illness or death, and ensure safe burial of carcasses per official protocols; dumping carcasses in rivers or open areas is prohibited. Public urged to avoid meat from unknown sources. Violations will attract action under the Prevention and Control of Infectious and Contagious Diseases in Animals Act, 2009 and other laws. Measures take effect immediately.

article.articleHeadline: India Targets Foot-and-Mouth Disease-Free Status in Nine States to Boost Dairy Exports
article.articleSummary: India aims for foot-and-mouth disease (FMD)–free status in nine states within two years to access Europe’s dairy market. The states, identified for consistently low outbreaks and completed vaccination cycles, would be certified by the World Organisation for Animal Health, aiding the PM’s 2030 goal. A vaccination-and-traceability drive cut FMD outbreaks from 105 in 2021 to 40 last year; 38 crore animals now carry 13-digit IDs, with OTP-based verification. Indigenous vaccines for FMD, Classical Swine Fever (CSF) and PPR have been developed; a domestically produced African swine fever vaccine was launched. US tariffs of 58% in 2025 did not prevent seafood shipments rising to Rs 73,891 crore in 2025-26, aided by FTAs with over 100 countries. Inland fisheries remain a policy gap (2% of exports) though production rose 147% since 2014; drone transport proposed. Odisha’s brackish-water shrimp potential highlighted; Rs 123 crore under PM Matsya Sampada Yojana funds research, with KVK networks mobilized.

Treatment typically lasts several months, so sustained community support aids completion and reduces drug resistance. article.articleHeadline: Climate crisis threatens Asia's fight to eliminate tuberculosis
article.articleSummary: Climate crisis threatens TB elimination in Asia, with Indonesia among the hardest-hit. In 2024, TB infected at least 10.7 million people and caused 1.23 million deaths worldwide; Asia houses most cases, with Indonesia accounting for about 10% and India ~25%. Overcrowding, poor ventilation, food insecurity and malnutrition worsen transmission and disrupt care during extreme weather. Dense urban settings, such as Mumbai, risk higher transmission as reliance on air conditioning reduces ventilation. Pakistan’s floods disrupted TB services, prompting courier delivery of medicines and diagnostics. Experts urge single-visit testing for TB and comorbidities, active case finding and latent TB identification. Indonesia detected about 885,000 of an estimated 1 million annual cases in 2024; roughly 150,000 undiagnosed. Indonesia aims for 65 per 100,000 by 2030, shifting to identify undiagnosed cases via mass screening in 13 Central/West Java municipalities starting July 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Evaluation of two inactivated vaccines against Campylobacter fetus in an experimental bovine model: immunological survey and genital clearance in heifers - Brazilian Journal of Microbiology
article.articleSummary: Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis (Cfv) causes bovine genital Campylobacteriosis, a venereal disease contributing to reproductive losses in natural-service herds. In Brazil, 44 heifers were allocated to four groups: G1 vaccine A, G2 vaccine B, G3 infected with placebo, G4 negative control. After intravaginal challenge with Cfv, animals were followed for 105 days. Culture of vaginal-cervical mucus showed lower positivity in vaccinated groups (G1 61.81%, G2 45.45%) versus G3 87.27% (p<0.05). Local IgA and systemic IgG responses were detected by ELISA in all challenged groups, with earlier increases in G1/G2. Agglutinating antibodies were observed post-vaccination, strongest in G2 (p=0.0316). qPCR indicated a lower bacterial load in vaccinated cattle during sampling. Conclusion: vaccines yielded significantly earlier clearance of Cfv from the reproductive tract, associated with elevated early humoral responses; vaccines merit field evaluation to assess reproductive performance.

article.articleHeadline: A deadly virus decimated Australia in the 18th century: it is believed to have been introduced by physicians, according to a study.
article.articleSummary: Smallpox decimated Aboriginal Australia in the late 18th century, likely arriving with the First Fleet that landed in Sydney in January 1788 to establish a penal colony. A new study tests two introduction routes—British settlers in Sydney or Indonesian fishermen in the north—using population, mortality, and migration data. Researchers propose the virus could have survived on variola crusts used for inoculation before the 1796 vaccine; crust powder from terminal patients rubbed into scratches. While Royal Navy ships did not routinely carry variola material, at least one surgeon may have obtained it en route near Rio de Janeiro or the Cape. There is no written evidence of deliberate dissemination, and Governor Arthur Phillip is unlikely to have orchestrated such an effort. Precolonial Aboriginal population now estimated at 2–3 million, not 200k–800k, with about 2.4 million additional deaths linked to disease and early 19th-century colonization.

article.articleHeadline: With four suspected measles cases, São Bernardo do Campo (SP) should vaccinate babies.

On July 9, frontline teams conducted a near-residence sweep: 520 visits, 800 interviews, and 89 immunizations given to those lacking complete vaccination. As of now, the state has seven confirmed measles cases, all imported. Dose zero does not replace routine vaccination; routine schedule remains: first MMR dose at 12 months, second at 15 months with tetraviral. People aged 1–29 should have two MMR doses; 30–59 at least one; health workers two doses.

article.articleHeadline: Court: Health insurance fund does not have to cover costs for possible leprosy in Brazil.
article.articleSummary: Telemedicine assessment costs for a suspected leprosy case diagnosed in Brazil were not preliminarily covered by a German statutory health insurance fund. In Germany, medical treatment is generally limited to the statutory benefits catalog, with foreign services allowed only in exceptional cases (Az.: L 16 KR 221/26 BER). The applicant, a 45-year-old woman diagnosed with leprosy in autumn 2023 in Brazil, sought coverage for medications and telemedicine treatment plus travel costs. The insurer refused, citing lack of a bilateral social security agreement and that entitlement abroad is suspended during stays. An initial injunction was denied; in April the Social Court ordered provisional payment. The Landessozialgericht Niedersachsen-Bremen reversed, upholding the insurer. It ruled telemedicine abroad can be claimed only in exceptional cases outside the EU/EEA, not met here, since leprosy was not sufficiently confirmed by tropical institutes or a Bundeswehr hospital. Tropical diseases are treatable at German tropical medicine institutes.

article.articleHeadline: Fiocruz completes domestic production of HIV medication; Maranhão already records 355 AIDS cases in 2026.
article.articleSummary: Dolutegravir, a key HIV antiretroviral, will be produced domestically in Brazil after Fiocruz completed technology transfer to Farmanguinhos from ViiV Healthcare (GSK). Anvisa authorization is pending before distribution through SUS can begin. Three lots have been produced and validated; quality-control analyses of the active pharmaceutical ingredient are underway to consolidate the national production chain. Since 2022 Farmanguinhos has supplied the SUS with over 739 million dolutegravir capsules produced at partner GSK facilities, and in 2025 began independent laboratory QC analyses. The new phase will also produce a fixed-dose combination of dolutegravir with lamivudine next year. In Maranhão, AIDS cases reached 967 in 2025, with 355 in the first half of 2026; São Luís (113), São José de Ribamar (51), and Imperatriz (34) are the leading 2026 municipalities. The WHO has recommended dolutegravir as first/second-line treatment since 2019.

article.articleHeadline: Global studies redefine the treatment of heart failure caused by Chagas disease
article.articleSummary: Chagas disease-related cardiomyopathy was studied in Parachute-HF (JAMA): 922 patients at 83 centers across Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Mexico were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril on top of guideline-directed therapy. Safety was comparable; no significant difference in cardiovascular death or first heart-failure hospitalization between treatments. However, sacubitril/valsartan achieved a markedly greater reduction in NT-proBNP at 12 weeks: median -30.6% versus -5.5% with enalapril, addressed by lead investigator Renato D. Lopes of Tribe MD. The Parachute-HF study, coordinated by the Brazilian Clinical Research Institute, is part of two landmark trials published in JAMA and JACC to provide disease-specific evidence for Chagas cardiomyopathy, enhancing guidance for the 30-40% of infected individuals who develop cardiac manifestations.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue cases rise in several of the country’s tourist destinations due to mid-year holidays.
article.articleSummary: July 16, 2026 update from Colombia reports 52,518 dengue cases in 2026 as of June 20, with 31,733 cases without warning signs, 20,241 with warning signs, and 544 classified as severe dengue. In the latest week, 2,778 new cases and 30 deaths were reported; 43 deaths are under investigation. Dengue transmission remains elevated in heavily visited tourist regions, with 61.1% of 2026 cases in Meta, Cesar, Bolívar, Santander, Norte de Santander, Magdalena, La Guajira, and Cartagena. Amazonas, Arauca, Atlántico, Barranquilla, Casanare, Guaviare, Magdalena, Meta, and Santa Marta also above transmission limits. Health experts warn that travel increases exposure to Aedes aegypti. Preventive measures after return include using repellent, long sleeves, eliminating standing water, nets, and seeking medical care for fever, headache, muscle pain, nausea, vomiting, or malaise.

article.articleHeadline: An Angolan biomedical researcher develops biomarkers that can identify malaria early.
article.articleSummary: Malaria biomarkers identified in Angola may enable early identification of patients at higher risk of complications. Angolan biomedical researcher Teresa Luzembo, who recently completed a master’s study at the Faculdade de Medicina de Ribeirão Preto (FMRP) of the University of São Paulo, investigated serum nanoparticle profiles and their relation to ABO blood groups, sex, and gestational status. Analyzing serum from malaria patients and healthy controls, the study measured the quantity, size, and physicochemical characteristics of serum nanoparticles—tiny structures that act as biological messengers. Results show nanoparticle profiles differ among groups and may correlate with ABO type, suggesting ABO blood type may confer protection against severe malaria forms. The findings promise a valuable tool for the Angolan health system in managing malaria.

article.articleHeadline: Users complain about lack of tests for COVID-19 and influenza in Curitiba's health units.
article.articleSummary: Curitiba, Brazil, faces winter-driven rises in COVID-19 and influenza activity. As of 2026-07-16, residents report testing shortages at Boqueirão and Ouvidor Pardinho health posts, though the Municipal Health Secretariat (SMS) confirms a testing protocol. COVID-19 tests are available to all units and exceed 5,800 in use with about 7,000 in stock; testing is offered to patients meeting protocol criteria, prioritizing high-risk groups such as pregnant people, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. The SMS did not provide numbers of tests performed. Influenza testing is not available in health units because influenza is not a mandatory-notification disease; surveillance relies on sentinel monitoring. Curitiba’s sentinel units—Urgent Care Units (UPAs) Campo Comprido, Cajuru, and CIC—collect weekly samples for the Paraná State Central Laboratory (Lacen-PR) to monitor circulating respiratory viruses. COVID-19 testing follows warning-symptom criteria, with red flags prompting care at Central Health or a health post.

article.articleHeadline: SII signs Gates MRI pact to manufacture promising TB vaccine candidate
article.articleSummary: On 16 July 2026, Serum Institute of India (SII) and Gates Medical Research Institute (Gates MRI) announced a manufacturing pact for M72/AS01E tuberculosis vaccine candidate. Pune-based SII will develop capacity to manufacture and supply the vaccine for high TB-burden countries, subject to ongoing Phase-III trials and regulatory approvals, enabling scalable, affordable production for low- and middle-income nations where TB remains a leading killer. TB causes over one million deaths annually worldwide. The M72/AS01E asset, developed by Gates MRI after licensing from GSK, is among the most advanced TB vaccines and could become the first new vaccine to prevent pulmonary TB in adults in more than a century, complementing BCG. SII’s deal follows other global partnerships this month, including a Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine Phase I trial by Oxford Jenner Institute, and dengue therapeutic trials involving Brazil, Malaysia, and Thailand. SII serves over 170 countries and aims for low-cost production at scale.

article.articleHeadline: Vall Companys will cut its investments and dividend in half in 2026 due to swine fever.
article.articleSummary: African swine fever (ASF) outbreak detected in Barcelona, Bellaterra on 28 November forced Vall Companys to deploy a contingency plan that included a 61 million euro provision to mitigate market closures and export blockages. In 2025, the group earned 4.626 billion euros in revenue (up 11%), but net profit fell to 245.4 million euros, down 12% from 2024. The plan expects 2026 dividends to be halved to 36 million euros and investments trimmed to 85 million euros, versus 193.2 million euros invested in 2024 for modernization. ASF remains a grave risk to the meat sector by depressing pig prices and constraining export markets. Despite this, flour and poultry divisions posted positive results, and pork exports reached 35% of sales, led by Central Europe, ahead of Asia. Vall Companys pursues Latin American growth: Chile in 2026 with Coexca/Master Agroindustrial and Argentina with Grupo Pacuca (14 million dollars loan). Since 2016, it has minority stakes in Peru, Colombia, Uruguay, Brazil; Mexico is 75% owned.

article.articleHeadline: Costa Rica Detects for the First Time a Virus in Ticks That Had Not Previously Been Identified in Central America.
article.articleSummary: Costa Rica and Central America report the first detection of Jingmen tick virus in ticks, found in Valle La Estrella, Limón. The virus was detected in Amblyomma mixtum ticks collected from horses (97 samples analyzed between Oct 2023 and May 2024); ticks from vegetation tested negative. There is no evidence the virus causes disease in people or animals in Costa Rica, and no diagnostic test beyond the PCR used in the study is available. Whether horses participate in transmission remains uncertain, though the virus could involve other hosts given the tick’s broad vertebrate range. Genomic analysis at the Pasteur Institute (France) reveals a local Costa Rican variant linked to Europe and Western Asia lineages, distinct from Brazilian African-associated lineages. No detections were found in Ciudad Colón, Heredia, Monte de la Cruz, or Vara Blanca; preliminary comparisons with Panama show regional viral differences. The finding prompts enhanced surveillance and prevention efforts.

The mother reported the child had no classic flu symptoms at first; fever developed within 48 hours and another convulsion occurred. By Thursday the 16th the child was responding to treatment.

article.articleHeadline: São Paulo confirms a case of avian influenza in a wild bird.
article.articleSummary: São Paulo, Brazil, confirms a case of avian influenza in a wild bird. The broader report, published 16 July 2026, analyzes how Brazil’s poultry sector must broaden indicators and transparency to track evolving international buyer expectations. Brazil remains the world’s largest exporter of chicken meat, but leadership depends on sustainability, traceability, health, and animal welfare integrated into supply chain practices, not only production efficiency. The Observatório do Frango (Alianima) uses SWOT to identify drivers of competitiveness: strengths include integrated production, quality and biosafety management, technical capacity, and readiness to adopt new technologies; weaknesses include limited transparency and fragmented coordination across chain links. Ongoing market pressures from Mercosur–EU talks and a push for origin, production processes, and environmental/social indicators push firms to formalize welfare metrics. About 1.5 billion birds are raised under higher-welfare densities, about 27.7% of national production. A collective, long-term leadership is urged to transform initiatives into measurable commitments.

article.articleHeadline: Suspected leptospirosis cases in Catanduva ruled out by the Adolfo Lutz Institute
article.articleSummary: As of 16 July 2026, suspected leptospirosis cases in Catanduva, specifically in the Nova Catanduva neighborhood, were ruled out after analyses by the Adolfo Lutz Institute, the official reference laboratory for São Paulo's State Health Secretariat. The investigation began following a preliminary screening test at a private lab; such tests are not definitive and require confirmation by an official reference method. Additional samples were collected by the Municipal Health Secretariat and sent to Adolfo Lutz. Results were negative for leptospirosis; one assay was inconclusive and is undergoing routine supplementary testing. Nevertheless, preventive actions and surveillance remain in place: the Zoonoses Surveillance Unit conducts rodent-focus inspections and educates residents, while the local health unit continues monitoring. The Health Secretariat reiterates rigorous investigation per Ministry of Health protocols. Residents are advised to keep yards clean, properly manage waste, avoid rodent habitats, and seek care if compatible symptoms appear after potential exposure.

article.articleHeadline: Diphtheria resurges in many parts of the world; JD Health Internet Hospital reminds: vaccination is the key, and seek medical care promptly for suspected symptoms.
article.articleSummary: Diphtheria resurges; Nigeria and Australia report cases since 2025, with outbreaks and case fatality up to 14.3%. China has had about two decades without locally acquired diphtheria, but importation risk remains. Caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, the disease can release toxins damaging the respiratory tract, heart, and nerves. Early symptoms resemble a cold, but red flags include fever, sore throat, and a gray pseudomembrane; membrane fragments can obstruct the airway between days 7–10. About 20% of cases are cutaneous or ocular. Transmission is by close contact; untreated disease has high mortality. Vaccination with diphtheria vaccines is the key preventive measure. China’s program since Jan 1, 2025 uses the DTaP schedule at 2, 4, 6, 18 months and 6 years, with boosters every 10 years; travelers should verify vaccination and may need pre-travel boosters. Seek prompt medical care for suspected symptoms; treatment includes antitoxin and antibiotics. JD Health Internet Hospital offers 24/7 online triage and AI-assisted guidance.

article.articleHeadline: Five-year-old girl infected with a 'superbug' is at risk due to sweet, cooling summer snacks that adults still love.
article.articleSummary: A five-year-old girl in Hong Kong contracted Shiga-toxin–producing Escherichia coli (E. coli O157:H7) after eating ice cream at a local restaurant during a summer trip to Zhanjiang, Guangdong, China. She presented with vomiting, diarrhea, and severe abdominal pain; laboratory tests confirmed E. coli infection with the Shiga toxin, raising risk of acute kidney injury. The Hong Kong Centre for Health Protection notes a 2–10 day incubation (typically 3–4 days) and that symptoms include diarrhea (often with blood), abdominal cramps, and dehydration. She was admitted to The Chinese University of Hong Kong Hospital; nephrology input and readiness for dialysis or plasma exchange were in place, but her condition improved by evening and she was discharged with home treatment. Officials warn ice-cream–associated E. coli infections can occur, especially in children during summer, underscoring safe handling of dairy products.

article.articleHeadline: Comprehensive analysis of the safety and protective efficacy of Sinovac's Vero cell-based hand, foot and mouth disease vaccine and Kunming Institute's human diploid cell-based vaccine
article.articleSummary: HFMD ranks second in nationwide infectious-disease incidence in June 2026 in China, with 257,993 cases, and July marks a summer peak. The core at-risk group is children ≤5 years, especially under 3, with EV71-driven HFMD capable of rapid progression to brainstem encephalitis or meningitis. EV71 vaccination for 6–71 months is an effective prevention strategy. The article notes that Vero cell–based and human diploid cell–based vaccines are different production substrates, not a quality hierarchy; WHO endorses parallel use of both. In Zhejiang’s Yiwu real-world study (n=6,854), no serious adverse events occurred; fever 3.0% (Vero) vs 3.5% (diploid); in 24–35 months, 2.5% vs 5.3% (P<0.001). Phase 3 head-to-head shows higher seroconversion with Sinovac Vero vaccine (95.5% vs 86.0%). Sinovac Erlai Fu’s ultra-low impurity profile yields rapid onset (10 days, 89.2% seroconversion) and durable protection to 64 months (~94%). Conclusion: both vaccines are effective; for faster, longer protection with lower reactogenicity, Sinovac Erlai Fu is preferred; begin at 6 months and follow local guidance.

article.articleHeadline: Don't underestimate them by thinking they're small; these creatures threaten human life.
article.articleSummary: Asian giant hornet (murder hornet), native to East Asia, can reach about two inches and stings with venom that can be fatal; several deaths are reported annually. Bullet ant, found in Central and South American rainforests, grows up to 1.2 inches; nests may have up to 3,000 individuals; its sting delivers extreme pain lasting 12–24 hours due to poneratoxin, though deaths are rare. Mosquitoes (Anopheles) transmit deadly diseases including malaria, dengue, and Zika virus. Kissing bug (Triatominae) vectors Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) via bite and defecation; infection can cause serious heart and digestive problems and may be life-threatening if untreated. Tsetse fly, common in southern Africa, transmits African sleeping sickness (Trypanosoma brucei), affecting the brain and nervous system. article.articleHeadline: Harbin Institute of Technology surveys 450 people infected with AIDS and finds that AIDS patients share four common characteristics.
article.articleSummary: Harbin Institute of Technology surveyed 450 people living with AIDS in Harbin, China, and identified four common characteristics. 1) Acquaintances are treated as safe; transmission occurs via bodily fluids regardless of relationship. 2) Post-exposure prophylaxis is treated as a backup, not primary protection; it is most effective within 72 hours of exposure, and missed doses reduce protection. 3) Health is judged by appearance; the HIV/AIDS window period can be up to three months, during which infection can be transmitted despite negative tests. 4) Testing is often delayed; more than 70% are diagnosed only 2–5 years after infection, allowing immune damage. Today ART can yield long life, but late treatment complicates care. Recommendations: maintain safe-sex measures, seek PEP within 72 hours, and use free anonymous testing at local CDCs with results in 10–15 minutes.

article.articleHeadline: Post-Flood Health Tips: Preventing Disease Risks
article.articleSummary: As of 17 July 2026, post-typhoon and flood conditions heighten infection risks from floodwater contaminated with microbes in garbage, feces, and animal carcasses. The National Health Commission advises drinking only boiled or disinfected water; avoid spoiled, moldy, or flood-soaked foods; wash fruits and vegetables with clean water and separate raw from cooked foods to prevent enteric diseases. Maintain a clean living environment by removing mud, standing water, garbage, and animal carcasses; disinfect surfaces and utensils, keep indoor areas ventilated, and ensure intact screens; use mosquito nets and coils to reduce vector exposure. In schistosomiasis-endemic areas, fever, diarrhea, or skin rash after floodwater contact should seek prompt medical care. Before summer travel, plan routes, monitor weather alerts, and avoid valleys or unfamiliar water bodies; if bitten by dogs or snakes, seek medical attention and note bite details. Wear easily removable clothing to prevent heat-related illness and hypothermia.

article.articleHeadline: Common Mistakes When Caring for People with Infectious Diseases at Home.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever, hand-foot-mouth disease, chickenpox, influenza, and measles are discussed in home care. Common mistakes include self-medicating with antibiotics for viral infections; antibiotics ineffective and drive resistance. Fever management pitfalls: avoid aspirin or ibuprofen in dengue or measles and avoid overdosing or combining oral and rectal dosing. Avoid extreme hygiene restrictions; bathe with warm water in a closed room to help cooling. Dangerous traditional remedies include cupping and applying leaves; risk of skin damage and infection. Home IV hydration is unsafe, especially for dengue; seek medical facility care. Practical advice: boost oral rehydration, light meals, monitor warning signs (persistent fever, lethargy, vomiting, breathing difficulties, bleeding) and seek hospital care when indicated. Context: home care guidance in Vietnam.

article.articleHeadline: 'Early-life armor' helps infants under one year reduce their risk of severe disease caused by RSV.
article.articleSummary: RSV infection in early infancy causes severe disease such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia, with risk persisting throughout the first year. Transmission occurs year-round via respiratory droplets and contaminated surfaces (toys, cribs, door handles). Infants aged 6–12 months remain vulnerable; a US study found 6–11 months had emergency department visits at nearly 77% of the rate seen in 0–5 months, and pediatric outpatient visits were about 14% higher. Data from Vietnam’s National Children’s Hospital show 6–12 months account for a high share of visits and hospitalizations, and natural immunity to RSV is not long-lasting, allowing reinfection. Prevention focuses on maternal vaccination to confer passive protection and monoclonal antibodies that directly protect newborns, including immediately after birth. Widespread protection can reduce infant hospitalizations, cut medical costs, and lessen healthcare system strain during peak respiratory seasons.

article.articleHeadline: Does Japanese encephalitis increase during lychee season?
article.articleSummary: Japanese encephalitis in Vietnam typically peaks May–July, aligning with lychee season, but fruit is not the source. Reservoirs include wild birds (waterfowl such as herons and egrets; cuckoo) with pigs as amplification hosts; Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes transmit the virus to humans. Transmission is not via eating lychee and there is no human-to-human spread. Incubation is 5–14 days (often ~7). Early manifestations: sudden high fever, headache, fatigue, vomiting; children may be irritable and eat poorly. Neurologic involvement causes neck stiffness, severe headache, vomiting, drowsiness, coma, seizures; fulminant disease can lead to meningitis, encephalitis, respiratory failure, multi-organ failure, shock, and death. No specific antiviral therapy; management is supportive. Prevention centers on vaccination and mosquito-control. Vaccines: Jevax (Vietnam) from 12 months via routine immunization with boosters every 3 years; Jeev (India) from 12 months via service vaccination with boosters during outbreaks or before exposure; Imojev (Thailand) from 9 months via service vaccination and does not require post-basic booster. Emphasize mosquito-bite precautions."

article.articleHeadline: TSPCA warns of emerging zoonotic diseases from animals to humans, and reiterates the need to care for animals with understanding.
article.articleSummary: Thailand’s TSPCA and Mahidol University’s Faculty of Veterinary Medicine warn of emerging zoonotic diseases jumping from animals to humans, a trend reflected in global data: over 60% of new human pathogens originate in animals, and more than 70% come from wildlife. Notable examples include novel influenza, avian influenza, SARS, MERS, COVID-19, and monkeypox. The spillover is driven by human-driven bridges—deforestation, habitat loss, dam and road construction, and expanded wildlife trade (legal and illegal)—which increase contact between people and diverse wildlife and facilitate viral exchange. The response emphasizes One Health: human, animal, and environmental health are interdependent. Public actions include avoiding wildlife contact, practicing hygiene (eat hot foods, use clean utensils, wash hands), maintaining tidy homes to deter pests, and responsible wildlife viewing (distance, no chasing, no feeding). The organizations advocate education on humane animal care to prevent cruelty and disease transmission.

article.articleHeadline: First domestic Zika virus infection case; Huang Wei-che urges citizens to take mosquito precautions.

Zika can be transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, sexually, and vertically, so men returning from outbreak regions should practice safe sex for three months and women for two months, using condoms or abstaining if the partner is pregnant. Pregnant women are advised to avoid Zika-affected areas. After returning, continue personal mosquito precautions for at least three weeks and defer blood donation for one month. Tularemia is a natural foci zoonosis transmitted by insect bites, contact with infected animals, and contaminated water or food. Symptoms include fever, headache, weakness, lymph node swelling, and sometimes buboes. Dacha owners should ventilate rooms, perform wet cleaning, and work on plots wearing a four-layer gauze mask and rubber gloves; protect homes, dachas, and cellars from rodents. Outdoor precautions include repellents, insecticides, light clothing and head coverings, and tick checks every 1.5–2 hours with careful removal. In late June, a Russian tourist returning from Thailand was diagnosed with melioidosis, prompting travel guidance for Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America: wear closed footwear, avoid freshwater bathing, avoid flood zones, and avoid contact with animals.

article.articleSummary: Chikungunya outbreak prompts CDC travel advisory for Costa Rica: local transmission in Playa Langosta, Santa Cruz, and Guanacaste with 45 suspected cases, 4 confirmed, and 17 possible per Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health. The U.S. Embassy notes Costa Rican nationals and foreigners are affected. CDC issues Level 2: Practice Enhanced Precautions; travelers should use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants, and stay in air-conditioned or screened accommodations. Vaccination is recommended for areas with outbreaks; pregnant women should not travel due to risk to newborns. In the United States, 2026 has 75 travel-associated chikungunya cases across the U.S. and territories. Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus; symptoms include fever, muscle pain, fatigue, and rash, usually resolving in 1–2 weeks, but severe joint pain can persist and requires hospitalization in infants or the elderly. Local transmission means the virus circulates in local mosquitoes, not only imported cases. Originating in Tanzania in 1952; name from Makonde language meaning the pain described by patients.

article.articleHeadline: Prevention needed to curb mosquito-borne diseases in the rainy season - Global New Light Of Myanmar
article.articleSummary: During Myanmar's rainy season, dengue fever transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, along with malaria, seasonal influenza, acute diarrhoea, dysentery, typhoid fever, and other respiratory infections, pose increased health risks. Health authorities urge preventive measures, including eliminating mosquito breeding sites and resting places, maintaining clean homes and surroundings, ensuring proper drainage, and practicing good personal hygiene with frequent handwashing. Public awareness campaigns should inform residents that Aedes mosquitoes bite mainly during the day and rest in dark indoor spaces, reinforcing bite-prevention strategies and regular inspections to remove breeding habitats. To curb diarrhoeal diseases, health messages stress safe water, clean food handling, thorough cooking of vegetables, fruits, meat, and fish. Overall, strengthening immunity through nutritious clean food and hygiene is emphasized, since prevention is presented as better than cure during the rainy season (as of 2026-07-16).
